attributes.title: Level 9

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you define a callScene function that checks if the number parameter is equal to 4 possible conditions inside the function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What are some User Interface (UI) features that you’ve seen before?

❓ What will the callScene function be used for in this project?   

❓ How do you define a function with a number parameter?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider the UI features that they’ve seen before and may already be familiar with (such as splash/game over screens, a choice menu, allowing the user to select their character, text that appears when a user interacts with something, etc.). Ask the ninja to consider how adding UI features to a project improves the User Experience (UX)  of a game.

💡 In this project, the callScene function will be used to display the various scenes on the screen. Scene 0 will be the splash screen, scenes 1 and 2 will be the 2 game levels, and scene 4 will be the game over screen.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation if they need help adding a number parameter to the function or adding the conditional code inside of the function.
steps.instructions:
Create a function to set up the various scenes in the project!


Notice that there is already code for a maze game in the project.


This game can be improved by adding User Interface (UI) features, including splash and game over screens, and a menu to allow the user to make a choice. 


This project will have 4 scenes: a splash screen, 2 maze levels, and a game over screen. Under // game set up, define a callScene function with a sceneNum number parameter. Add a conditional inside the event with 4 possible conditions that check if the parameter is equal to 0, 1, 2, or 3.

steps.hints: ❓Did you call the callScene function with the correct scene parameter to test scene 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the callScene function is called and 1 is passed as the argument?

❓ Why do you think scene 0 was skipped in this step? What code might go there?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the callScene function is called with 1 passed as the argument, Player and Goal sprites will be placed on random tiles on the level 1 tilemap and the Player sprite will be set to move with buttons.
steps.instructions:
Reorganize the starter code inside the function!


Cut and paste the code that creates the Player and Food sprite into the callScene function definition, before the if conditional.


Cut and paste the code that sets the tilemap, places the sprites, and sets the Player sprite to move inside the condition that checks if sceneNum is equal to 1.


Under // game set up, call the callScene function, passing 1 as the argument. 


Click ▶ to see the Player and Food sprites appear in the level 1 tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the argument in the function call to see both maze levels appear on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should be updated to test out level 2?

❓ What happens when the callScene function is called and 2 is passed as the argument?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to pass different arguments (1 and 2) in the callScene function call to test out both levels of the game.

💡 When the callScene function is called with 2 passed as the argument, Player and Goal sprites will be placed on random tiles on the level 2 tilemap and the Player sprite will be set to move with buttons.

💡 Explain to the ninja that while the levels in this game will be simple, their main focus will be on creating engaging assets and User Interface (UI) features throughout the project that will improve the user’s overall experience.
steps.instructions:
Code the second level of the maze!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen and notice the 2 tilemaps and 2 spawn tile assets that are used for the 2 different levels. 


Return to the JavaScript editor, then copy all the scene 1 code and paste it inside the else if condition for scene 2. Then, update the tilemap and tile assets names.


Click ▶ to see each level by updating the argument and calling the callScene function.

steps.hints: ❓Did you call the choiceMenu function if sceneNum is equal to 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the Story extension be useful in this project? 

❓ What is the choiceMenu function used for?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of how they’ve used the Story extension in the past. In the last Purple Belt level, they used the choice menu from the Story extension to ask the user to select their difficulty level for the game and to print text on the screen. In this level, the choice menu will be used again as well as other story extension functions. The choice menu engages the user and creates a personalized experience.

💡 The choiceMenu function will be used to ask the user which level they’d like to play in the game.
steps.instructions:
Use the Story extension to create a menu of levels that the user can choose from!


Click Extensions then scroll down to add the arcade-story extension to the project.


Define a choiceMenu function. Open Story and drag [show player choices (choice1) (choice2)] inside the function definition. Use showPlayerChoices to ask users to select a level by typing “Level 1” and “Level 2” inside the parentheses.


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum is equal to 0, add a // choice menu comment, then, call the choiceMenu function.

steps.hints: ❓Did you call the callScene function after checking the user’s choice inside the choiceMenu function definition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the choiceMenu function is called?

❓ What value is stored in the currentScene variable?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the choiceMenu function is called, the user will be asked to select Level 1 or Level 2. Then, the project will check what the user’s response is and call the callScene function, loading the scene that matches the user’s response.

💡 The currentScene variable stores the number that matches the user’s response. This number will be passed to the callScene function so that the user is presented with the level number that they chose.
steps.instructions:
Create the 2 possible game conditions that will happen as a result of the user’s choice.


Under // project initialization, create a currentScene variable set to 0.


Under // game set up, pass the currentScene variable as the argument in the callScene function call.

 

Create an if/else if conditional inside the choiceMenu function definition. 


Open Story and drag [last answer equals (choice)] inside the parentheses of the if and else if conditions. Type the string “Level 1” inside the parentheses of the if condition, and “Level 2” inside the else if condition. 


Set the currentScene variable to 1 in the if condition, and 2 in the else if condition.


After the if/else if conditional checks the user’s choice, call the callScene function, passing currentScene as the argument.


Click ▶ to see the menu offer 2 choices to the user.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use sprites.destroy() to remove the duplicate Player and Food sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do the Player and Food sprites need to be destroyed before a game level is loaded in the callScene function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the Player and Food sprites are created at the top of the callScene function, in order to access them in each of the below conditions. As a result, Player and Food sprites are created in Scene 0, as well as in Scene 1 or 2. This creates a double set of sprites, which causes the game to end immediately when they overlap.
steps.instructions:
Destroy the Player and Goal sprites after the menu screen appears. 


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum is equal to 0, destroy the Player and Food sprites after the choiceMenu function is called.


Click ▶ to test that duplicate sprites do not appear on screen after the menu choice has been made.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use setKind to set a sprite kind for the text sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the Text Sprite extension be used for? 

❓ What do the foreground and background color parameters in the textsprite.create function represent?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja that the Text Sprite extension is useful for creating a string of text that remains on screen. The extension has many text sprite customization functions, such as setting its outline,font size/style, border, and image icon.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the foreground parameter of the textsprite.create function represents the color of the text and the background parameter represents the color that appears behind the text. Have the ninja consider what colors to use for each parameter, to make the text clearly stand out on screen.
steps.instructions:
Use the Text Sprite extension to add a title to the game menu!


Click Extensions, then scroll down to add the arcade-text extension to the project.


Open Text Sprite and drag [text sprite (text)] under // project initialization. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

let textSprite = textsprite.create("")

The textsprite.create function takes 3 parameters: text, background color, and foreground color. Give the text sprite a descriptive name, and keep the text parameter as empty ‘’ so it can be updated in different scenes. Select contrasting color values for the foreground (color of the text) and background (color behind the text). 


Create a Title sprite kind for text sprites, then set the text sprite’s sprite kind as Title.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use one of the sprite functions to position the text sprite on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What number might you set the text sprite’s font height to? 

❓ How do the font styles change as the font’s height is changed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the Text Sprite extension creates text sizes that are multiples of 5 or 8. Any other number used as the argument in the setMaxFontHeight function will not change the size of the text. If the ninja is unfamiliar with the concept of multiples, provide a few examples for 5 (5, 10, 15, 20) and 8 (8, 16, 24, 32) that they can tinker with in their code.

💡 If the font size is a multiple of 5, it will have a different font style than if it is a multiple of 8.

💡 Point out to the ninja that a text sprite is still a sprite, so any sprite functions can still be used on it (such as setKind, setPosition, destroy, etc.).
steps.instructions:
Update the text, size, and position of the text sprite!


Open Text Sprite and drag [set (textSprite) text (text)] into the choiceMenu function definition, before the if/else if conditional and showPlayerChoices function. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

textSprite.setText("")

The setText function takes 1 parameter: text. In the choiceMenu function definition, set the text parameter to “Choose a Level”.


Open Text Sprite again and drag [set (textSprite) max font height (height)] underneath the code that sets the text. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

textSprite.setMaxFontHeight(0)

The setMaxFontHeight function takes one parameter: height. Set the text sprite’s height to 8.


Set the text sprite’s position so it appears at the top center part of the screen.


Click ▶ to test the size of the text sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the outline color so that the text is contrasted by the outline color?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What color might be used as the text sprite’s outline?

❓ What might the text sprite’s x and y-positions be set to, so that it appears at the top center part of the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they should use a color that will create a clear contrast between the text and the background image to outline the text sprite. Have the ninja tinker with the color parameter to see how different outline colors appear on screen.
steps.instructions:
Customize the outline of the text sprite.


Open Text Sprite and drag [set (textsprite) outline) (1) (6)] underneath the code that sets the size of the text sprite. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

textSprite.setOutline(1, 6)

The setOutline function takes 2 parameters: width and color. Set the width parameter to 1, then tinker with the color parameter to set an outline for the menu title.


Click ▶ to test the outline and position of the text sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the text parameter to empty "" in the the setText function to reset the text sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should the text parameter be set to in the setText function, in order to cause the text sprite to “disappear”?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The text parameter should remain blank (without any text between the quotation marks) in order to make the text sprite “disappear” when the next scene loads. Point out to the ninja that this is a useful strategy for reusing the same sprite later in the project, so that the sprite doesn’t need to be destroyed.
steps.instructions:
Oh no, the text sprite stays on screen even after the next scene loads!


Open Text Sprite and drag [set (textSprite) text (text)] into the choiceMenu function definition, after the conditional. 


Set the text parameter to empty "" before the callScene function call.


Click ▶ to see the text sprite reset once a maze level has been selected.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the colors of the text sprite so it shows up against the splash screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the splash screen background image show? What color might you use for each layer? 

❓ What details might you add to blend each layer together and make them distinct?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider background images that are already in the gallery. What similarities and differences are noticeable between them? Have the ninja brainstorm what kind of scene they’d like the splash screen to represent (such as an outdoor or indoor scene, a specific place, or an abstract image). Then, have them identify different colors to use (both complementary and analogous) to create contrast and smooth the transitions between the layers. 

💡 Point out the different tools in the paint editor that can be helpful for designing a 160x120 image. The zoom in/zoom out tools on the bottom right corner can be helpful for focusing on one area of the image at a time. The marquee tool is useful for rearranging a specific part of the image. The canvas pan tool can also be used to drag the image around the editor to see the different parts of the image more closely. The ninja can also select different brush sizes to draw at different scales.
steps.instructions:
Design an image for the splash screen!


A splash screen appears at the beginning of the game. It generally will feature the title of the game and show a preview of the scenes or characters that appear in the game. 


Create a 160x120 image asset in the Assets menu for the splash screen. Name the image asset splashScreen. 


Start by using solid colors to create clear layers in the background image, defining the foreground and background of the scene. Add details in the image to add to the theme (such as stars in the sky, flowers in the grass, sparks in a flame, or waves in the ocean).


Then, use pixel art techniques (such as dithering, complementary colors, and highlights/shadows) to add depth to each part of the image. Consider which aspects require the most detail and which can be left mostly solid. Use tools in the paint editor (such as zoom in/out, marquee, and canvas pan) to focus attention on one part of the image at a time.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the splashScreen’s sprite kind as Background?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is a splash screen used for in a game? How does it engage the user?

❓ Why is it useful to separate the Scene 0 code with comments?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 A splash screen is a useful UI feature in games because it immediately captures the user’s attention. Splash screens typically have an engaging background and sprite images that give the user a sneak peak into what they might expect from the game. Small pieces of the splash screen may be animated to further hold the user’s attention on screen. This is a great place to add a title and any other immediate directions that the user will need.

💡 Point out to the ninja that there will be several parts of the first scene (Scene 0): background image, text sprite, animation, and the choice menu. Because there are many different types of functions being run, it’s useful to use comments to organize the different sections.
steps.instructions:
Create a Background sprite that can be animated for this project.


Create a new Background sprite kind.


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum is equal to 0, add a // splash screen comment above the existing code. 


Create a new Background sprite named background underneath. The splash screen is a sprite instead of a background image so that it can be animated in the next step. 


Destroy the Background sprite after the choiceMenu function is called so it is removed before the maze tilemaps are displayed on screen.


Click ▶ to see the splash screen appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the Show Previous Frame tool to compare the different frames?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What parts of the splashScreen asset might animate to engage the user?

❓ How quickly might the Background sprite animate on the splash screen? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja identify 1 or 2 parts of the background image that would make sense to animate. These might be small details (such as stars in the sky) or features that might have movement in real life. Prompt the ninja to use the Show Previous Frame tool to see where the image was moved in the previous frame to create clear movement across the frames.
steps.instructions:
Create an animation for the splash screen.


In the Assets menu, select the splashScreen asset and click Copy under the Asset Preview pane. Create a splashAnim animation asset, then paste the image into the first frame in the animation paint editor. 


Duplicate the frame to create a total of 3 frames, adjusting details in each frame so that the scene comes alive. 


Return to the JavaScript editor and code the Background sprite to animate in the callScene function definition if sceneNum is equal to 0. Update the runImageAnimation parameters accordingly.


Click ▶ to see the animated splash screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the text sprite height to a value that is a multiple of 5 or 8 and larger than the choice menu text?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What size might you set the text sprite’s text to? 

❓ What color might be used to outline the text sprite so that it creates a clear contrast with the background image?

❓ What might the text sprite’s z-property be set to?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the Text Sprite extension creates text sizes that are multiples of 5 or 8. Any other number used as the argument in the setMaxFontHeight function will not change the size of the text. If the ninja is unfamiliar with the concept of multiples, provide a few examples for 5 (5, 10, 15, 20) and 8 (8, 16, 24, 32) that they can tinker with in their code.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out different colors in the setOutline function to create a clear contrast between the text sprite and the background image.
steps.instructions:
Customize the title of the splash screen.


Inside the callScene function definition when sceneNum is equal to 0, add a // text sprite comment below the Background sprite code. 


Open Text Sprite and add the setText, setMaxFontHeight, and setOutline functions underneath. Update the text with the name of the game. Tinker with the font height so the title of the game appears larger. 


Set the text sprite’s position so it appears at the top center part of the screen. Set the text sprite’s z-property so it appears in front of the Background sprite.


Click ▶ to test the size, outline, and position of the text sprite on the splash screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you place the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function before the choiceMenu function is called?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function do? Why might it be useful in a project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function pauses the project until a user presses a button. This is useful for creating a title screen that the user can view, then when they’re ready, they can press a button to begin the game.

💡The pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed function is a secret menu function that can only be accessed by typing controller and a dot operator, then selecting the function from the code completion tool.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The game title does not show up since the menu title appears immediately!


Underneath // choice menu, type controller and a dot operator, then select pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed from the code completion tool. Type a pair of parentheses () to call the function. 


Click ▶ to see the game title appear with the animated splash screen, and then change to the menu screen when any button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with the Player sprite’s z-property so it appears in front of the Background sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What animation asset might be used to animate the Player sprite in the first scene?

❓ Where might the Player sprite be placed on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can view the Gallery to select a premade animation asset for many of the sprite images. Have the ninja select an animation that the user will view in the first scene of the project.
steps.instructions:
Create an animated Player sprite asset.


In the Assets menu, create a playerAnim animation asset. Select an animated asset from the Gallery that matches the player sprite from the starter code.


Return to the JavaScript editor. Inside the callScene function definition, under the condition if sceneNum is equal to 0, add a // player sprite comment before the // choice menu code. 


Code the Player sprite to appear near the middle of the screen, update the z-property so it appears in front of the Background sprite, and set it to animate. Update the runImageAnimation parameters accordingly.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite animate on the splash screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the text sprite height to a value that is a multiple or 5 or 8?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the callScene function is called with 3 passed as the argument?

❓ Why is it useful to include comments inside the scene 3 conditional?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the  callScene function is called with 3 passed as the argument, a blank tilemap will be set, the splashScreen asset will be displayed on screen with “You Win!” text, and the Player sprite will appear animated.

💡 Point out to the ninja that there will be multiple parts of the fourth scene (Scene 3): the win screen and an option for the user to play again. Because there are many different functions being run, it’s useful to use comments to organize each section.
steps.instructions:
Add a game over screen!


Inside the callScene function definition, inside the condition if sceneNum is equal to 3, add // win screen. 


Under // win screen, add code to set the tilemap to empty ‘’ and create another Background sprite set to the splashScreen asset. Reset the Player sprite’s position so it appears in the middle of the screen and animates. 


Use the setText and setMaxFontHeight functions to set the text to say “You Win”. 


Add a screen effect and a sound to accompany the game over screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the value of currentScene before calling the callScene function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite?

❓ What symbol should be used to reassign the value of the currentScene variable?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite, both sprites will be destroyed, the currentScene variable will be set to 3, and the callScene function will be called with 3 passed as the argument.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation for help with reassigning the value of a variable.
steps.instructions:
Update the onOverlap code so the Game Over screen will load!


Inside the onOverlap event from the starter code, delete the gameOver function. Set the value of the currentScene variable to 3. Call the callScene function, passing currentScene as the argument.


Click ▶ to test that the Game Over screen appears once the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the title parameter of the game.ask function to say something such as “Play Again?”?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens if the user wants to play again?

❓ What UI features do you notice are added in this step?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the user wants to play again, they can respond to the game.ask() screen to reset the game.

💡 Point out to the ninja all the different UI features that are added to this step that improve the game’s experience. A sound, screen effect, and user response are all ways to engage the user and improve their experience. By destroying the sprite’s and calling the choiceMenu function, the project is initialized to begin from the starting point, without having to view the title screen again.
steps.instructions:
Create an option for users to play again.


Inside the callScene function definition, under the condition if sceneNum is equal to 3, add a // play again comment. 


Use pauseUntilAnyButtonIsPressed to pause the project until the user is ready to move on.


Use a game.ask() function to ask users if they would like to play the game again. Then, end the screen effect,  call the choiceMenu function, and destroy the Background, Player, and Goal sprites.


Click ▶ to test the prompt for the user to play again.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use setKind to set a sprite kind for the scoreText sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the scoreText sprite need to be declared under // project initialization?

❓ Why is it useful to create a text sprite to show the score?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The value of the score variable will be updated later in the project in functions and events. As a result, if the variable and sprites were declared inside of those functions, they would be unable to be accessed anywhere else in the project, due to scope. As a result, it’s necessary to create a global variable by declaring the variable and sprite at the beginning of the project.

💡 Point out to the ninja that this is another way of adding a variable to a game. By using a text sprite instead of the default score function, the ninja is able to personalize how the variable appears and acts on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Use a scoreText sprite to display a score variable on screen!


Another User Interface (UI) feature that improves the experience is giving feedback to the user about the game, such as providing a score once a Goal sprite has been collected.


Under // project initialization, create a score variable set to 0. Use the textsprite.create function to create a scoreText text sprite. Set the text parameter to empty ‘’ so it can be updated throughout the project. Update the foreground and background color parameters. Then, set the sprite kind to Title.

steps.hints: ❓Did you pass the score variable as the argument of the convertToText() function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What else might a game variable be used for in a game?

❓ What does the convertToText function do? Why is it necessary?

❓ What will happen when the createVariable function is called? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the createVariable function is called, the score will be reset to 0 which will be updated on screen with a new border, icon, and position.

💡 The convertToText function converts a numeric value into a string value, so that it is able to be passed to the setText function. Because the value stored in the score variable is a number, the convertToText function must be used.

💡 If the ninja has created a tilemap larger than the size of the screen, have the ninja turn the RelativeToCamera sprite flag on for the sprite. This will keep the variable stationary and visible in the top corner of the screen.
steps.instructions:
Create a function to place the custom score variable on screen.


Define a createVariable function. Open Text Sprite and add the setText function underneath. Because the text parameter will only accept a string, type convertToText() as the parameter to turn the score number variable into a string. 


Set the scoreText sprite to be positioned at the top left or right of the screen. 


Call the createVariable function under // game set up then click ▶ to see the scoreText sprite appear on screen. Adjust the coordinates of the position as needed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you tinker with the setBorder function parameters so that the score variable shows up against the background?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do the setBorder and setIcon functions do? How might they be used in a project? 

❓ What icon might be used for the scoreText sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The setIcon function sets an image icon next to the text sprite, which can be updated based on what the text sprite is being used for. The setBorder function draws a border around all of the text sprite’s characters. The width, color, and padding parameters can be updated to personalize the border’s appearance.

💡 Prompt the ninja to recall what the default score and life variables look like on screen. The score value appears in pink with a white background and a pink border. The life value is shown by 3 heart images with a white background and a pink border. With this information, ask the ninja to consider how they might personalize the color and the icon of the scoreText sprite to create an engaging image on screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a border and an icon to the custom score variable. 


Open Text Sprite and drag [set (textSprite) border (1) (6)] underneath the code that sets the text. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

textSprite.setBorder(1, 6)

The setBorder function sets the scoreText sprite’s border. It takes 3 possible parameters: width, color, and padding. Tinker and set the width and color parameters to create a box around the score display text. 


Open Text Sprite and drag [set (textSprite) icon (icon)] underneath the setBorder code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

textSprite.setIcon(img` `)

Replace img` ` with the Food sprite image asset name.


Click ▶ to see the updated scoreText sprite on screen. Adjust the width and color of the border as needed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an increment operator ++ to increase the score variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol should be used to increased the score variable?

❓ What will the score show on the screen when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation if they need help identifying the symbol to increase the score variable by 1.

💡 Now, when the Player sprite overlaps the Food sprite, the score will be updated on screen.
steps.instructions:
Update the score after each round of the maze! 


Inside the onOverlap event, increase the score variable by 1 after the Player and Food sprites are destroyed. 


Then, use the setText function to update the score, using the convertToText() function to change the score variable value into a string.


Click ▶ to test if the score updates correctly.

steps.hints: ❓Did you make any changes that might improve the project?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What else might be added to improve the User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) of the project?

❓ What is one new feature that you learned from this project that you want to add to future games?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to identify the various features that they coded in this project and how that impacted the game’s overall feel and experience. Encourage the ninja to think more about what else could be changed or added to make this a full game with even more UI features in it.
steps.instructions:
Playtest the project! 


Playtest the project and notice how the User Interface (UI) features improve the User Experience (UX)  of the project. 


Think about how text, menus, and background screens were used in this project. Consider what other changes might be made to create additional levels, a “lose” screen, or other UI enhancements.

subgroups.title: Maze Masters
subgroups.introduction: Create a project with custom splash and game over screens, and a menu for players to choose a level from.

validationItems.text: Use a callScene function with a sceneNum parameter to call the different scenes in the project.
Create a menu of choices for the user to select from.
Use a currentScene variable to call a specific project scene based on the user’s choice.
Use text sprites to create on screen text.
Set the text sprite’s string, max font height, position, and outline.
Create a 160x120 splashScreen image asset to use as the project’s splash and game over screens.
Create an animated version of the splash screen image.
Pause the current scene until the user presses any button.
Ask the user if they wish to play again after the game over screen.
Display a score variable as a text sprite by converting the value to a string. Update the value at the end of each level.
Add a border and icon to the score variable display.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 9 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about adding User Interface (UI) features, such as splash and game over screens, user choice, and game narrative that can significantly improve the User Experience (UX) of a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 9:

badges.title: Screen Time
badges.description: Use a variety of pixel art techniques to create full-screen image assets to enhance the user experience in a project.

badges.title: An Asset for Every Season
badges.description: Create 160x120 full-screen image assets that can be layered on top of one another to create a variety of game screens.

badges.title: Flavor Text
badges.description: Use the Text Sprite extension to create custom scene titles, directions, and variable counters on screen.

badges.title: Choose Your Adventure
badges.description: Create a personalized experience for the user by changing scenes based on their responses.

badges.title: Reliable Narrator
badges.description: Use the Story extension to create narrative scenes that describe what’s happening in the project.

badges.title: Chain of Command
badges.description: Convert a number value to a string.

badges.title: Red Light Green Light
badges.description: Pause a project until any button is pressed to make screens remain as long as a user chooses.
